title: Asma's belt
hook: Abu Bakr's daughter Asma tears her waistband in two to tie the food bags, and is called she of the two belts (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cave of Thawr: two men hidden in the dark, searchers at the mouth. Your line was: two, and Allah the third. When did you feel less alone than you looked? Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

A food bag, a water skin, and no string. That is the whole problem in today's story, and it happens in a house in Mecca on the night two men are about to vanish. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and Abu Bakr are leaving for Yathrib in secret. Somebody has to pack the food. In Sahih al-Bukhari it is Abu Bakr's daughter, Asma, who tells us what happened in that kitchen. The meal is ready. The bags are ready. And there is nothing in the house to tie them shut. Today: Asma's belt.
screen: `NO STRING.` → `A SECRET NIGHT.` → `ASMA IN THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Here is the scene as Asma tells it in Bukhari. She prepared the journey food for the Prophet and her father. They looked for something to bind the food bag and the water skin, and found nothing. So she said to her father, in effect: by Allah, I can find nothing to tie it with except my waistband. And Abu Bakr answered: then tear it in two. Tie the water skin with one half and the food with the other. She did. And from that night on, she says, she was called dhat al-nitaqayn: she of the two belts. Look at how small the solution is. No miracle, no clever plan. A young woman uses the cloth already wrapped around her. The great journey of the hijrah, which we have been following for days, leaves the house tied shut with half of a waistband. Notice too where she is standing. The men are hidden in a cave. Asma is the one still in the city, still in the house the searchers will come to. The sirah tells of her carrying food out to the cave in the nights that followed, so her part was not finished in the kitchen. And look at the name she earned. It doesn't remember a speech or a battle. It remembers a quick, practical choice made with what was in reach. Aisha's telling of the night, also in Bukhari, puts it a little differently: Asma cuts a piece of her belt rather than tearing it in two. Both keep the same picture: the bag closed with her own cloth. The road to Medina did not begin with what anyone wished they had. It began with what was there.
screen: `NOTHING TO TIE THE BAGS.` · `TEAR IT IN TWO.` · `SHE STAYS IN THE CITY.` · `A NAME FOR A PRACTICAL CHOICE.` · then, large: `SHE OF THE TWO BELTS.`

segments.voice: The practice: use what you have. Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind one thing you've been putting off because you don't have the right tool, the right time, or enough of something. Hold it there for a breath. Now look at what is actually around you: in your room, your pocket, your day. Ask quietly: what here could tie this bag shut? Not perfectly. Just well enough to start. If you pray, you can ask Allah for help with what is already in your hands. Let one small answer come, and stay with it. The bell holds the time.
Asma's belt. Torn in two on the night of the hijrah to tie the food and the water, it gave Asma her name: she of the two belts. Today's word.
Your line: two belts. Today, when you catch yourself waiting for the right thing, reach for the thing already in reach and tie the bag shut. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims retell Asma bint Abi Bakr's part in the hijrah from Sahih al-Bukhari and know her by the name it gave her: dhat al-nitaqayn, she of the two belts.

myth: Asma left Mecca with the Prophet and Abu Bakr
she stayed in the city; the two men hid in the cave.
in Bukhari, Asma herself tells the story of the belt
she describes preparing the food and finding nothing to tie it with.
every report in Bukhari says she tore the belt in two
in Aisha's account she cut a piece of it; in Asma's own, she tore it in two.

fork.setup: you're Asma. the food is ready, the travelers leave tonight, and there's nothing in the house to tie the bags. what do you do?
options: send someone out to find rope.
tear your waistband in two and tie them.
let them go with the bags open.
fork.reveal: Abu Bakr told her to tear it in two, one half for the water skin, one for the food, and the name stuck: she of the two belts.

original.note: Arabic: 'she of the two belts', the name Asma was known by.

trapdoor: what you thought: a small detail about packing a lunch.
what it means: the hijrah left the house tied shut with a torn waistband, and Asma earned her name for it.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 2979 and 3907, in Asma's own report; Aisha's long account in 3905 says she cut a piece of her belt.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2979 (Asma prepares the food; nothing to tie it; 'tear it in two'; called dhat al-nitaqayn)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3905 (Aisha's account of the hijrah; Asma cuts a piece of her belt)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Asma brings food to the cave)

notes: Bukhari numbers 2979, 3905, 3907 cited from memory; confirm.
In 2979 it is Abu Bakr who tells Asma to tear the belt in two; the index hook says Asma tears it. Script follows the hadith wording. Confirm.
'Carrying food out to the cave in the nights that followed' is attributed to the sirah; confirm (Ibn Ishaq; Bukhari 3905 names Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr and Amir ibn Fuhayra for the nightly visits).
'A young woman' is descriptive, no age given; confirm appropriate.
Audit pass: 'Bukhari's other reports' (only one other is cited) now names Aisha's account; replaced the filler myth about buying cord with the real difference between the two reports.

Editor pass: 'every version keeps the same picture' became 'both' (only two reports are cited); howItsDone no longer claims she is invoked 'especially when speaking of women's roles', which no cited text supports.
